prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength condition and its realisation as a many-atom frequency standard at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my single part, and after the second reading I hold it with somewhat more confidence on the question the chair put first, whether it is a new invention. The comb of 2005 gave us a ruler that counts optical cycles. The ion work of 2012 showed how to control and read out a single quantum system. Neither tells you how to hold thousands of neutral atoms, with their statistical power, in a standing wave of light without the light itself shifting the clock transition. Katori's magic wavelength answers exactly that: the ground and excited states are shifted equally, so the perturbation cancels where it matters. That is a new physical condition, not a smaller error bar. It is also what made the later steps possible: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, control of collisions and many-body effects in the lattice, and clock comparisons between independent laboratories at the 10^-18 level (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE). Because it has been reproduced and surpassed by others, I do not rely on a single measurement. A Katori-Ye prize also credits an idea and its decisive realisation with a clean two-name lineage. The citation I propose names the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realisation, not a precision record, so that the Yb, Hg and ion-clock communities are not read as excluded and the prize does not become a prize for a number.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection with the 2005 and 2012 prizes has not gone away and I cannot prove to a sceptic that the committee will see the step as a discovery of nature. The attribution objection is also real: Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups made essential contributions to the 10^-18 milestone, and any two-name prize leaves some of them out. I have not seen the 2001-03 priority record and my memory of who proposed what, and when, is not good enough to settle it, so an outside expert check on the magic-wavelength priority and on Ye's specific contributions is a precondition, not a formality. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the largest consequence is still ahead. I count that as neutral for timing, because the prize is for what the clock has already shown, but I understand colleagues who count it the other way.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B004 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a new symmetry-protected state of matter with nearly two decades of confirmation, and asks how much weight a better measurement tool should have against the discovery of a new state of matter.
responses.response: I take the question seriously and I do not think the answer is that matter always outranks instruments. Band theory felt finished, and the Z2 classification showed it was not; that is a real surprise and it is the sort of thing I like. But your own file concedes the credit is untidy (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang with the HgTe proposal, Zhang's death, Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan for three dimensions) and that the 2016 prize is close in subject. I would find a prize with a visible gap harder to defend than one whose two names cover the concept and the realisation. In that sense the clock is the cleaner configuration, though I would not call it the more important physics, and I keep B004 as my second alternative because the HgTe experiment is a decisive quantitative test. Where I can move is this: if outside experts show that the BHZ proposal is not a separable step from Kane-Mele, then B004 becomes a stronger competitor than I have given it credit for.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B009 (MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero) as the only shortlisted case where the field is still opening, and concedes that B006 is the more mature, more cleanly attributed alternative; she asks how the citation can avoid claiming an explanation of the superconductivity.
responses.response: Your acknowledgement that the clocks are the safer choice is fair, and I would answer your point about openness this way: the lattice clock is still opening too, since many-body clock physics, tests of fundamental constants and searches for dark matter are active. I agree that the moire phenomena are real and widely reproduced and your wording, which stays with observed correlated insulators and superconductivity, is the right way to cite them. My remaining difficulty is the one you name yourself: eight years of history, an open pairing mechanism and an experimental first author who cannot be named. I would rather wait to see which moire results are the lasting core. I do defer to you and Mehlig on whether the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is already decisive, since this is not my field, and I do not think a B009 prize would be a mistake. I think it would be early.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to B006 and asks whether a single two-person prize is the best use of the year or whether a second distinct part could be added without exceeding three laureates.
responses.response: I considered the second part. With Katori and Ye already two names, a second part would leave room for one person only, and none of the shortlisted achievements has a defensible single name: IceCube depends on a collaboration and on Halzen and Spiering together, the cold-atom prize needs at least three of five, and circuit QED has the Wallraff problem. Adding someone only to fill the quota would weaken the attribution that makes B006 attractive. So I keep a single part. I also agree with your point that priority at the 10^-18 milestone should be checked with an outside report rather than recalled from memory, and I would support asking for that before the vote.

responses.point: Kroll agrees on B006 and says the citation should name the concept and the 10^-18 realisation so that the Yb, Al+ and other clock groups are not read as excluded, and he asks for an expert check of the 2001-03 priority.
responses.response: We agree and my citation now follows your suggestion in its wording. Your disclosure about the year in Hall's laboratory is, in my view, a limited concern as you have no collaboration with Katori or Ye; I would leave the question of recusal to the chair and the committee and would not ask you to step back. On our one difference, you prefer tests of relativity and control of many-body effects to a technological promise, and so do I. I would keep the words 'frequency standard' in the citation because that is what the device is, but not metrology, geodesy or redefinition of the second, which are consequences and not the discovery.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B043 (Halzen, Spiering) with less certainty than in his opening and says that if outside reports cannot settle who was decisive, B006 is the cleaner prize.
responses.response: That is a candid position and I think it is correct that the attribution question in B043 cannot be answered from the openings. I agree that the 2013 diffuse flux is an observation that has been seen independently, and I would not demand that every source be identified before the prize is considered. But Baikal, DUMAND and AMANDA make a two-name credit of a collaboration of hundreds hard to defend without an expert report, which you say yourself. You have also said that a B006 prize is the cleaner alternative, which I take as a statement of where the committee could meet. I leave IceCube outside my alternatives only because astroparticle physics is outside my competence and I do not want to rank it on a view I cannot defend.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice clock as an invention distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-clock recognitions; I think it is, but this is a judgement and not a measurement.

The 2001-03 priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal and the specific weight of Ye's contribution against Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups; I rely on memory and want an expert report.
If B006 fails, I would turn to B023 or B004, but I have not resolved which three of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac, or how the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap would be handled.
I cannot judge the condensed-matter and astroparticle cases in detail and rely on colleagues on their maturity.
statement.conflict_note: No change. Katori, Ye and the other credited names are not among my listed collaborators. I am a close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and work in atomic, molecular and optical physics, which is near the clock and cold-atom candidates, but I do not see that as a reason to recuse. I note Kroll's disclosure about JILA-adjacent work and agree with him that it should be decided by the chair and the committee. I would accept their ruling on mine.
